$comment: A worked plan.json. Written after round 0 came back green and collect-graph-context.js had run, before any version was changed. Every 'graph_evidence' value here names something that was actually in graph-context.json — that is what makes the prediction different from a guess.
title: Spring Boot 3.5.0 to 4.1.1 on Java 21
summary: This moves the employee service from Spring Boot 3.5.0 to 4.1.1 and from Java 17 to Java 21. Boot 4 brings Jackson 3, Spring Framework 7 and a reorganised actuator package with it, so roughly six source files have to change even though no business logic does — the code graph shows the application touching the framework in exactly three places, and those are the three places expected to break. The REST contract is not expected to change at all, and five probes replayed on both runtimes will show whether that held. Best estimate is four to six build rounds over half a day, with the main uncertainty being the test layer, which cannot be compiled until the main code is clean.
drivers: Spring Boot 3.5.x leaves open-source support in mid-2026; security patches after that are commercial-only.
Java 21 is the LTS the Boot 4 generation is built and tested against, and the release the container base image already offers.
Jackson 2.x, pulled in transitively today, has no fix branch for the deserialization advisories tracked against it.

architecture_reading.summary: The graph shows a single-module application with 14 types, one REST controller exposing 5 endpoints, and only three types coupled to anything defined outside the repository. That is a small framework surface for an application this size, and it is why the predicted change list is six files rather than sixty — most of the code never names a Spring type at all.
framework_coupling: `DatabaseHealthIndicator` implements `HealthIndicator`, an external type — the actuator health package is one of the things Boot 4 relocates, so this file is the single highest-confidence prediction in the plan.

`JacksonConfig` is annotated `@Configuration` and builds an `ObjectMapper` directly, which is the Jackson 2 type; the graph shows nothing else constructing a mapper, so the JSON change is contained to this one file plus its two test usages.

`EmployeeController` exposes all 5 endpoints and has 4 dependents in the graph — it carries the whole REST contract, so it is the file where a behavioural regression would be most visible and the one the probes cover most heavily.
blind_spots: The graph has no edge for `application.yml`, so property renames between generations will not appear anywhere in it — those surface at runtime, not at compile time, which is why the readiness probe matters as much as the build.
The Dockerfile's base image and the CI workflow's Java version are ancillary files the graph does not model at all; both were read from baseline.json instead.
Nothing in the graph is marked stale, so the semantic layer above was written for this shape of the code.

phases.name: Build file and coordinates
phases.goal: Move the parent, the language level and the renamed starters, and let the resolver tell us what no longer exists.
expected_failures: Unresolvable artifacts for starters that Boot 4 split or renamed
Missing packages where Jackson 2 types were imported
graph_evidence: The graph lists 11 declared dependencies on this module; 3 of them are starters the reference pack flags as renamed.

phases.name: Main source — JSON and health
phases.goal: Follow the compiler through the relocated packages and changed mapper API until main compiles.
expected_failures: `ObjectMapper` configuration methods that no longer exist on the Jackson 3 type
graph_evidence: Exactly 2 types touch these APIs — `DatabaseHealthIndicator` (implements `HealthIndicator`) and `JacksonConfig` (@Configuration).

phases.name: Test layer
phases.goal: Bring the tests onto the new test starters and mocking annotations. Tests only compile once main does, so this phase cannot start earlier.
expected_failures: Removed test annotations in the three test classes
Mapper type mismatches in the controller test
graph_evidence: The graph covers main source only; the three test classes were read from disk to size this phase.

predicted_changes.what: Parent version to 4.1.1, java.version property to 21, three starters renamed to their Boot 4 coordinates.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 splits spring-boot-starter-web by stack and modularises the test starters.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The graph's DEPENDS_ON edges list all 11 declared coordinates for this module.

predicted_changes.what: Import and implement the relocated HealthIndicator/Health types.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 moves the actuator health contract to a new package root.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The only type in the graph with an IMPLEMENTS edge to the external type `HealthIndicator`.

predicted_changes.what: New Jackson 3 package root and mapper builder API.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 carries Jackson 3, which changes the package root and the configuration entry point.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The only @Configuration type in the graph that constructs a mapper.

predicted_changes.what: Replace the removed test annotation and update the health assertions.
predicted_changes.why: The test annotation it uses is removed in Boot 4 and the health document's shape changed with the package move.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Not in the graph (main source only) — read from disk alongside the health indicator it exercises.

predicted_changes.what: Base image to a Java 21 JRE.
predicted_changes.why: The language level moves to 21, so the runtime image has to carry a JDK that can run the artifact.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Not modelled in the graph — listed in baseline.json's ancillary files.

predicted_changes.what: Possibly a renamed actuator or Jackson property.
predicted_changes.why: Property renames between generations do not appear at compile time and only surface when the application starts.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The graph has no edge to configuration, so this one is a reference-pack prediction with nothing behind it.

dependency_plan.reason: The generation jump itself — every managed version underneath follows from this one.
The LTS the Boot 4 generation is built and tested against.
Boot 4 splits the web starter by stack; this application is servlet-based.

risks.risk: The actuator health document changes shape, so anything scraping /actuator/health sees a different payload even though no application code changed.
risks.mitigation: The health endpoint is in the probe list and its body is compared before and after; any difference is reported as a client-visible change rather than rounded down to 'unchanged'.
risks.graph_evidence: The graph shows `DatabaseHealthIndicator` contributing to that endpoint, and it is one of the two types that must change.

risks.risk: A configuration property is renamed, so the application compiles and starts but behaves differently.
risks.mitigation: The readiness check plus five endpoint probes run against the actually-started application on the new runtime, not just against the build.
risks.graph_evidence: The graph has no configuration edges at all, so nothing in the round loop would ever surface this.

risks.risk: The test layer needs more work than forecast and the migration stalls after main compiles.
risks.mitigation: The test phase runs its own rounds with `package`, and every round is recorded — a stall is visible in the ledger rather than hidden.
risks.graph_evidence: The graph covers main source only, so the test-layer estimate is the least evidence-backed number in this plan.

behaviour_plan.summary: The same five requests are replayed against the running application on Java 17/Boot 3 before anything changes and on Java 21/Boot 4 once the build is green. Status codes must match exactly; a body that differs with the same status is judged and explained rather than assumed benign.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees
probes.why: The happy path and the shape of the collection response.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees/1
probes.why: Single-resource serialization — the most likely place a Jackson change shows.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees/99999
probes.why: The error contract. A framework upgrade can change the default error body.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees (no auth)
probes.why: The authentication boundary — Spring Security 7 comes with the jump.

probes.name: GET /actuator/health
probes.why: The endpoint whose implementation is being changed.

not_covered: No scheduled or background work exists in this application, so nothing time-driven is checked.
Load and latency are not measured — the probes prove the contract, not the performance.

effort.estimated_duration: half a day, assuming both JDKs are installed and the first BOM download is not counted

rollback: Nothing in the project changes until the very last step. If the applied result is bad, `node scripts/apply-migration.js --slug spring-boot-3-to-4 --revert` restores every overwritten file from the pre-apply backup.
out_of_scope: No refactoring, renaming or reformatting — the diff should contain only what the upgrade forced.
No unrelated dependency bumps; a library that resolves fine under Boot 4 is left at the version it is on.
The three pre-existing TODOs in EmployeeService are left exactly where they are.
No change to the database schema or to the seed data.
open_questions: Is 4.1.1 the release you want, or should this wait for the next patch?
The health document's shape is expected to change — is anything on your side parsing it that we should warn first?
Half a day is the estimate; is there a window where the project should not be in a half-migrated state?
